query.query: can two pytest sessions run at the same time here

baseline_items.text:
Two pytest sessions running at the same time against the same test database collide. `tests/conftest.py`
calls `apply_migrations` from a session fixture, and `recall.schema`'s guard refuses the second one:

recall.schema.ConcurrentMigrator: another RE-call schema migrator is already running

The loser does not fail one test. **Every** test errors at setup, so the run reports e.g.
`3 skipped, 62 errors` with no failures at all. Reproduced deliberately on 2026-08-05 with three
concurrent runs of `tests/test_bench_systems.py`: one passed, two errored wholesale.

**Why it matters:** the guard is working as designed, but its failure signature looks exactly like a
catastrophic breakage of the code under test. It cost me a wrong conclusion once: in a mutation-testing
harness I counted two mutants as "caught" because the suite went red, when the redness was this
collision and not the mutant.

**How to apply:** run pytest sessions in this repo **sequentially**, never overlapping. In any harness
that shells out to pytest in a loop, treat `errors` and `failed` as different evidence: only `failed`
means a test caught something. Retry (or abort) on seeing `ConcurrentMigrator` in the output rather
than scoring that run. See also [[bench-systems-suite-spends-openrouter-credits]] for the other trap in
this same file.

---

| Symptom | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `ConcurrentMigrator` in fixture setup | two pytest processes contend for the schema-migration advisory lock; `scripts/ablate_store_latency_guards.py` documents it |
| `LockNotAvailable: canceling statement due to lock timeout` | another session on the SAME container, still running |
| `test_rate_limit_http.py`, `test_mcp_auth_http.py` | these stand up real HTTP servers and contend on PORTS; a private container does not protect them |
| `FileNotFoundError` inside `tmp_path` | pytest keeps only the 3 most recent `pytest-of-<user>/pytest-<n>` roots and prunes older ones AT STARTUP, so a new run deletes the dirs of runs in flight |
| pool / latency / backend-count assertions ("pool churned: 3 distinct backends…") | CPU contention, not DB contention |
|

Measured 2026-09-01 on this workstation. A full `python -m pytest tests/ -q` run ended
**2 failed, 898 passed, 13 skipped in 652s**, both failures raising from `harness/sandbox.py:181`:

```
RuntimeError: git add failed in sandbox ...\pytest-16129\test_informed_reference_passes11\sandbox
(exit 128, timed_out=False): fatal: Out of memory, malloc failed (tried to allocate 1048576 bytes)
```

The two were `tests/test_damage_detection.py::test_no_detector_fires_on_a_recorded_factless_session[ts-natural-order]`
and `tests/test_references.py::test_informed_reference_passes[ts-dedup-order]`. Re-running **just
those two selections** immediately afterwards gave **45 passed, 5 skipped** with no change to the
tree. Free physical memory at that moment was 2,289 MB of 16,375.

**Why this

**Moved here 2026-08-15** from the `RE-call` memory store, which forked from this one when the
directory was renamed to `recall`. It sat there unreachable for ten days while I worked the same
failure family from the other store. Renaming a project directory silently forks its memory.

The collision is narrower now but not gone: `scripts/session-db.sh up` gives each checkout its own
database, so two sessions in *different* checkouts no longer contend for one migrator. Two runs in
the *same* checkout still do, because they share a DSN. The reading rule survives intact and is the
durable part: **`errors` and `failed` are different evidence, and only `failed` means a test caught
something.** See [[concurrent-pytest-false-reds]].

```
5694 passed, 32 skipped in 1857.08s (0:30:57)
```

`CLAUDE.md:140` states "The full suite takes about **12 minutes** with a database and about 5

independent defects lined up to turn "the suite did not finish" into "the suite passed".

query.query: what happens if I mix two embedding models in one tenant

baseline_items.text:
🔑 **One embedding model per tenant.** Not a convention: it is the only thing standing between a
mixed corpus and silently wrong retrieval. When a corpus wants a code model and a prose model,
that is two tenants, not one with two writers.

Found on 2026-08-15 designing the `recall_repos` corpus on VPS2 (five repositories, code via
`voyage-code-3`, docs via `voyage-4`). Ten tenants, `<repo>-code` and `<repo>-docs`, for exactly
this reason. The index driver asserts `code_embedder.dim == docs_embedder.dim` before writing,
because both tenants share one table and one fixed vector width.

⚠️ The same reasoning applies to the CHUNKER, but the failure is different and worse: see
[[chunker-is-not-in-the-index-fingerprint]]. Related: [[guards-that-cannot-fail]],
[[recall-corpus-name-boundary]].

`RetrievalDiagnostics.embedding_profile` (`recall/retriever.py:325`, `:471`) is **reported, never
enforced**. Nothing in `recall/store.py` filters rows by it: the only occurrence is a `count(*)
FILTER (WHERE NOT metadata ? 'embedding_profile')` used for a readiness report. So a tenant holding
passages from two models is not an error state the code can see.

It is also not a *loud* failure, which is the part that matters. pgvector would reject a dimension
mismatch, so two models of DIFFERENT width fail fast. The dangerous case is two models of the
**same** width: `voyage-4` and `voyage-code-3` are both 1024, so a query embedded with one is
cosine-compared against passages embedded with the other, the SQL succeeds, and the ranking is
garbage that looks exactly like a ranking.

So a live memory search embeds the query with voyage-4 and compares it against 8,716 bge-small
document vectors. **Both models emit 1024 dimensions, so pgvector computes a cosine happily** and
returns a confidently ranked list that means nothing. No error, no warning, no failure code that
names it.

Re-measure (the profile lives in the row's metadata, and mixing shows up as more than one value):

```bash
psql "$RECALL_DSN" -c "SELECT tenant_id, metadata->>'embedding_profile' AS profile, count(*) \
  FROM chunks GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1,3 DESC;"
ssh vps2 "ps -eo args | grep -o 'RECALL_TENANT=[^ ]* RECALL_EMBEDDER=[^ ]*' | sort -u"
```

Related: [[generation-tenants-are-invisible-to-the-legacy-store]] (whose "0 rows in chunks" claim
this session corrected), and [[recall-env-development-bypasses-the-generation]].

---

✅ **Resolved 2026-08-22 by converging the CORPUS, not the client.** The `memory` tenant was
re-embedded with `voyage:voyage-4`, the model `~/.codex/config.toml` already queries it with, so all
three layers now name one model. The two candidate fixes were not equivalent:

🔑 **Verify an embedder by `vector_dims(embedding)`, never by the profile label**: at least on
the fastembed path. Extends [[mixing-embedders-in-one-tenant-is-silent]]: the field that was
supposed to make mixing detectable is itself inert, so that lesson is stronger than written.

Not filed as a fix yet. The fix is to derive the default `profile_id` from model name plus
dimension, which re-fingerprints every fastembed corpus, a migration, not a one-liner.

query.query: will re-indexing repair a chunker bug

baseline_items.text:
**The chunker is not in it.** So a file whose bytes have not changed is skipped even when the
chunker that would now read it is a different one. Fixing a chunker-selection bug therefore does
**not** repair an affected corpus by re-running `recall index`, the run reports "N unchanged" and
leaves every wrongly-split chunk exactly where it was.

To actually rebuild, change one of the three terms (a different embedder, a different context
policy) or delete the affected sources first and let the next run re-read them.

The source docstring calls widening the tuple out as a migration rather than a comment change,
because it re-fingerprints every indexed corpus at once. That is a real cost and the reason it has
not been done, not an oversight.

Found on 2026-08-15 fixing `recall index`, which chose the chunker from the GLOB SUFFIX
(`chunk_code if args.glob.endswith(".py") else chunk_text`) rather than per file, so
`--glob '**/*'` chunked every `.py` as prose and said nothing. Fixed by `chunker_for_path`, with
the non-repair noted in its docstring so the next person does not assume a re-index is enough.

⚠️ `chunk_code` is **Python-specific**: it starts a block at a column-0 `def`/`class`/`@`/`async
def`. Given Rust, SQL or shell it matches nothing, returns one block, and is strictly worse than
`chunk_text`, which at least splits on blank lines. Do not widen `PYTHON_SUFFIXES` without a
chunker that parses the language being added.

## Two consequences measured 2026-08-18

**Decision, 2026-08-18: deferred deliberately.** Not a bug and not a to-do. Recorded so that a
future session does not "helpfully" re-index it, and does not read the mismatch as corruption.

## Why deferring is safe, which is the part that is easy to get wrong

- **The corpus keeps serving correctly.** `index_fingerprint` is only ever compared to ITSELF by
  the incremental skip guard. No retrieval path, no trust gate and no readiness check reads it, so a
  stale value degrades nothing.
- 🔁 **Calibrations are NOT at risk, correcting what I first told the user.** Measured 2026-08-18:
  no calibration path reads `index_fingerprint` at all (`grep index_fingerprint` over
  `calibration.py`, `calibration_v2.py`, `generations.py`, `trust.py` returns nothing). v1 binds to
  `EmbeddingProfile.fingerprint()`, which `79a0d6ed` did not alter, and v2 binds to a generation.
  The code and memory corpora calibrated on 2026-08-18 stay valid across a re-index.
- **The re-embed would produce identical vectors**, because the embedder, the text and the chunker

1. Retract **inside** the paragraph, in its first sentence. Not above it, not at the top of the file.
2. Keep the wrong claim rather than deleting it, so the direction of the error survives.
3. **Re-index, then re-run the query that surfaces the claim, and read what comes back.** The first
   two fixes here both looked correct in the file and were wrong in the index. An edit to a memo is
   not done until retrieval has been observed, and the observation is one tool call.

Cost: two failed corrections of the same paragraph, caught only because the query was re-run instead
of the file being re-read.

baseline_items.text:
As of 2026-08-12 this repo has ~18 worktrees. The main checkout at
`C:/Users/gde00/Documents/recall` usually sits on a feature branch (`codex/enterprise-rag-bench`
when this was written), and **`master` is checked out in a separate worktree at
`C:/Users/gde00/Documents/recall-suite-fix`**.

So `git checkout master` from the main checkout fails with *"'master' is already used by worktree
at ..."*. To land work on master, operate on that worktree directly:

```bash
git -C "C:/Users/gde00/Documents/recall-suite-fix" merge --squash <branch>
```

**Why:** 2026-05-03 backlog-drain session in worktree `frosty-hypatia-89f509` chained: `git checkout claude/hungry-hofstadter-d24e22` → rebase → `git checkout claude/frosty-hypatia-89f509` → `git checkout -b fix/paper-trades-unique-accession-index` → push → later `git fetch + git checkout -b deploy/sync-master origin/master`. After the last step, `ls` returned empty, `scripts/deploy.sh` 404, `git status` reported "nothing to commit" but `git reset --hard HEAD` left the tree empty. Worktree was effectively destroyed (also auto-pruned from `git worktree list`). Recovered the deploy by `cd`-ing to the main repo (`C:/Users/gde00/Documents/progetto sentimental`) and running `bash scripts/deploy.sh paper_trader.py --no-branch-check` from there.

**How to apply:**
- For PR work that needs branch checkout (rebase, edit, push): use a NEW dedicated worktree via `git worktree add`, OR cd to a non-Claude worktree (the main repo / the user's primary clone), OR ask the user to run it.
- To merge a PR via gh CLI: stay on whatever branch the worktree was already on; `gh pr merge --squash` doesn't need a local checkout. Skip `--delete-branch` if the target branch is held by another worktree (it errors otherwise).
- To deploy: cd to the main repo path and use `--no-branch-check` if it's on a transient branch label rather than literal `master`.
- If the corruption already happened: don't try to recover this worktree. Use a sibling worktree or main repo.

**Why this bit me:** I ran `git checkout master 2>&1 | tail -2 && git merge --squash <branch>`. The
pipe made `&&` read `tail`'s exit status, not the failed checkout's, so the squash merge ran against
the *feature branch* that happened to be checked out, leaving 13 staged additions and two
conflicted files in the user's working tree. `git reset --hard HEAD` restored it because nothing was
committed and the tree had been clean.

**How to apply:** Check `git worktree list` before assuming any branch can be checked out. Never
pipe a command whose exit status gates a `&&` chain; capture the status explicitly instead. And
check the target worktree is clean before merging into it.

query.query: what is wrong with a guard I wrote that always passes

baseline_items.text:
`scripts/session-mcp-close.sh` has a guard that stops it killing the ssh it is itself running,
whose command line necessarily contains the pattern it searches for. The tests had a fixture row
for exactly that process, the suite was green, and **deleting the guard kept it green**.

The reason is the interesting part. The fixture parented that ssh to `__SELF__` (the script's own
pid) but never put `__SELF__` itself in the process table. So the ownership walk failed at the
first hop and the process was excluded for **the wrong reason**: not "it is mine", but "its parent
is unknown". Every assertion still passed with the real guard removed. The repair was one fixture
line placing the script under the session client, which is where it really sits.

**Why:** a test that arranges the *shape* of a hazard without its *preconditions* asserts nothing.
Green means the code under test never reached the branch, and a passing suite cannot tell you that.

**How to apply:** for any guard, mutate it away and watch a named test go red before believing the
test. When one survives, suspect the fixture before suspecting the assertion, and ask what the walk
or the check actually did with that input rather than what it was supposed to do. Record the
MEASURED reds in the test header, not the predicted ones: on the sweep suite the measured set was
consistently wider than my prediction, because a mis-selection also shows up in the CLI tests.

🔑 The sharper version of the standing lesson: *a guard that reads as protection and cannot fire*
has a twin — **a guard that cannot PASS**. Both look like rigour in a document and neither tests
anything. Asking "what would make this fire?" catches the first; **"what would make this pass?"**
is the question I was not asking.

anything shipped — by the audit, not by me.**

baseline_items.text: Before deploying any sudoers lockdown that replaces wildcard `NOPASSWD: ALL` with a Cmnd_Alias allowlist, **verify whether the target user has a password set**. Without one, sudo for any non-allowlisted command silently fails with "a terminal is required to read the password" — the operator is locked out of every ad-hoc admin operation, and even console root login becomes the only recovery path.

**How to apply:**
- Step 0 (always): `sudo passwd -S <user>` (or `sudo grep <user>: /etc/shadow | cut -d: -f2`) — if it shows `L` / `*` / empty hash, no password is set.
- If no password: ask the operator before deploy, *"do you want me to set a password first (so non-allowlist commands prompt + work) or accept that the allowlist is a hard wall?"*. Do not assume.
- Even when a password exists, double-check the operator can recover via console — every Cmnd_Alias deploy needs a documented break-glass path that's been tested.
- Keep the pre-deploy file backup at a path the new sudoers still permits to read (so post-deploy rollback to the prior policy is possible from the same shell). The 2026-05-05 deploy left the backup at `/etc/sudoers.d/90-sentiment.bak.<TS>` — DENIED to read by the new

**Why:** 2026-05-05 redteam fix session. Saw `/etc/sudoers.d/90-sentiment: sentiment ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL` and assumed "NOPASSWD" implied "no password set". Deployed Cmnd_Alias lockdown. User immediately hit `[sudo] password for sentiment:` prompts when running outside the allowlist (e.g., `tee /etc/contabo/credentials.env`, `docker compose up -d` for a config refresh). The password actually *was* set, but the user couldn't remember it — equivalent to no fallback. Recovery options collapsed to (a) Contabo VNC console root login (operator did not have access at that moment) or (b) a destructive snapshot revert (the 2026-05-05 attempt got 400/404 from the Contabo API depending on body shape — `{}` body returns 404 'Cannot POST', empty body returns 400 'body cannot be empty').
